fixes.before: single hour for a contested event
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.623-624 (Chamberlain: near 4 p.m. the movement began); time-facts R066
fixes.find: label:"20th Maine — Col. Chamberlain held the extreme left of the Union line here at 4:30 PM July 2"
fixes.repl: label:"20th Maine — Col. Chamberlain held the extreme left of the Union line here from about 4:30 PM July 2; the hour of his bayonet charge is contested (about 5:10 to after 7 PM)"

fixes.before: count and anecdote stated as fact
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.623-624 (Chamberlain: the 15th and 47th Alabama prisoners); Oates 1905 account not re-read
fixes.find: label:"15th Alabama — Col. Oates made 4 assaults up this slope. Company B sent for water never returned."
fixes.repl: label:"15th Alabama — Col. Oates attacked the left of the 20th Maine repeatedly; Oates later wrote that he made several assaults (the count of four and the story of the company sent for water are from his postwar account, not the reports)"

fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.245 (Doubleday: Reynolds shot "in the beginning of the attack", about 10.15; Archer captured)
fixes.find: label:"Iron Brigade — Charged into Herbst Woods at 10:00 AM July 1. Archer captured."
fixes.repl: label:"Iron Brigade — Charged into Herbst Woods about 10:15 AM July 1 and hurled Archer's brigade back across the run; Archer was captured"

fixes.before: single hour for a contested time
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.245, p.696; ledger WSD-14
fixes.find: label:"General Reynolds killed here at 10:15 AM July 1 — directing the Iron Brigade into position"
fixes.repl: label:"General Reynolds killed here about 10:15 AM July 1 (Doubleday; Howard gives 11:15) — directing the Iron Brigade into position"

fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.429 (Webb), p.240 (Hunt); time-facts R114
fixes.find: label:"Lt. Cushing fired his last rounds here at 3:00 PM July 3 — killed at the moment of Armistead breakthrough"
fixes.repl: label:"Lt. Cushing, wounded in both thighs, fought on here and was killed at the fence by his guns during the assault, about 3:30 PM July 3 (accounts 3:00 to 3:45)"

fixes.before: anecdote as fact; 3:15 PM
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.428 (Harrow); time-facts R115
fixes.find: label:"Armistead fell here at Cushing's guns — July 3, 3:15 PM. Asked that his watch be delivered to Hancock."
fixes.repl: label:"Armistead fell here at Cushing's guns about 3:35 PM July 3 and was left mortally wounded within the Union lines (Harrow). Later accounts say he asked that a message and keepsake go to Hancock; that is tradition"

fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.366 (Hancock's dispatch of July 3: 'I was shot with a tenpenny nail. I did not leave the field till the victory was entirely secured'), p.117 (Meade); time-facts R115
fixes.find: label:"Hancock wounded here at 3:20 PM July 3 — nail driven into his thigh. Refused to leave until victory certain."
fixes.repl: label:"Hancock wounded here about 3:30 PM July 3 (Meade reports Hancock and Gibbon both severely wounded). His own dispatch says he was shot with a tenpenny nail and did not leave the field until the victory was secure"

fixes.before: text described the 140th New York on Little Round Top
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.157 (roster: 140th Pennsylvania in Zook's Third Brigade), p.375 (Roberts killed on the 2d)
fixes.find: label:"140th PA — Part of Vincent brigade that raced up Little Round Top just ahead of Law."
fixes.repl: label:"140th PA — Zook's brigade, II Corps; fought in the Wheatfield on July 2, where its colonel, Richard P. Roberts, was killed"

fixes.before: right of the brigade
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.632 (83rd Pennsylvania: "the Forty-fourth New York on my right, the Twentieth Maine on my left")
fixes.find: label:"83rd PA — Held the right of Vincent brigade on Little Round Top."
fixes.repl: label:"83rd PA — Held the left center of Vincent's brigade on Little Round Top, between the 20th Maine on its left and the 44th New York on its right"

fixes.before: tradition as fact
fixes.src: tradition, labelled
fixes.find: label:"Irish Brigade — Advanced into the Wheatfield with green boxwood sprigs, Celtic tradition before battle."
fixes.repl: label:"Irish Brigade — Advanced into the Wheatfield; regimental tradition says the men wore sprigs of green boxwood in their caps"

fixes.before: "greatest ... of any regiment" unqualified
fixes.src: Fox p.26, p.36, p.402; ledger WSD-12
fixes.find: label:"1st Minnesota — Charged Wilcox brigade to buy 5 minutes — lost 224 of 262 men. Greatest loss percentage of any regiment."
fixes.repl: label:"1st Minnesota — Charged Willcox's brigade on Hancock's order to gain time; Fox counts 224 casualties of 262 engaged for the battle (215 on July 2), the highest percentage of any Union regiment in a single battle in his tables"

fixes.before: implied the 72nd held the wall
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.374 (Hancock: the 69th and 71st behind the low stone wall, the rest of the brigade behind the crest)
fixes.find: label:"72nd PA — Webb's Philadelphia Brigade held The Angle against Pickett's Charge."
fixes.repl: label:"72nd PA — Webb's Philadelphia Brigade held The Angle against Pickett's Charge (the 72nd stood behind the crest; the 69th and 71st held the wall)"

fixes.before: 714 of 800; "highest ... on either side" as fact
fixes.src: Fox p.555-556; ledger WSD-13
fixes.find: label:"26th NC — Lost 714 of 800 men on July 1 — highest regimental casualties in the battle on either side."
fixes.repl: label:"26th NC — Fox: over 800 men engaged (820 present), 86 killed and 502 wounded, 588 in all (71.7 percent), most on July 1 with further loss on July 3; among the heaviest regimental losses of the battle"

fixes.before: no source for the flanking charges
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.350 (Stannard)
fixes.find: label:"16th Vermont — Made two separate flanking charges during Pickett'?s Charge. First day of combat."
fixes.repl: label:"16th Vermont — Under Stannard's orders changed front twice against the flanks of the Confederate columns during Pickett's Charge, taking the colors of the 2nd Florida and 8th Virginia. First day of combat."

fixes.before: 232 surrendered "in the wheat field" (the 232 belongs to the Railroad Cut)
fixes.src: OR 27/2 p.444 (Ewell: "The Twentieth North Carolina, being on the right of his brigade, suffered least"), p.554 (Rodes)
fixes.find: label:"Iverson's Pits — 20th NC advanced without skirmishers into an ambush. 232 surrendered in the wheat field."
fixes.repl: label:"Iverson's brigade, Oak Ridge — the 20th NC served in the brigade whose attack was cut down by musketry from the stone wall; many of the brigade's men were surrounded and captured"

fixes.before: 2:30 PM; anecdote as fact
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.728-729 (Schurz: "about 3 o'clock"), OR 27/2 p.445, p.469
fixes.find: label:"Barlow wounded here at 2:30 PM July 1. Gordon gave him water. They became friends after the war."
fixes.repl: label:"Barlow severely wounded here about 3 PM July 1 and captured (Schurz, Ewell). The story that Gordon gave him water, and of their later friendship, is from Gordon's own account"

fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.276 (Dawes); time anchor R017
fixes.find: label:"6th Wisconsin — Charged the Railroad Cut at 10:30 AM July 1. Captured 232 men and the 2nd MS flag."
fixes.repl: label:"6th Wisconsin — Charged the Railroad Cut about 11 AM July 1. Sent 7 officers and about 225 men to the rear and took the 2nd Mississippi's flag"

fixes.before: wrong text of the note ("It was my fault") and "in blood"
fixes.src: tradition (docs-copy-33); OR 27/2 p.319 (Avery commanding Hoke's brigade)
fixes.find: label:"Avery mortally wounded here during the assault on Cemetery Hill. His last note, written in blood: It was my fault."
fixes.repl: label:"Avery mortally wounded here during the assault on Cemetery Hill. The note attributed to him is traditional: Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy"

fixes.before: Stuart's purpose, the four brigades, the 7th Michigan and the quotation stated as fact; "stopped Stuart cold"; "no longer any rear to strike"
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.916 (Pleasonton), OR 27/2 p.322 (Lee)
fixes.find:
JEB Stuart's cavalry attempted to reach the Baltimore Pike and strike Meade's rear. Four Confederate brigades — Hampton, Fitz Lee, Chambliss, and Jenkins — advanced toward the Union rear.

Gregg's Union cavalry division, reinforced by Custer's Michigan brigade, blocked the advance. The 23-year-old George Armstrong Custer charged Hampton's brigade at full gallop with the 7th Michigan, shouting "Come on, you Wolverines!"

The collision of the two cavalry forces stopped Stuart cold. Hampton was wounded. By the time Pickett's Charge had failed, there was no longer any rear to strike. Stuart withdrew, and the East Cavalry Field action passed largely unnoticed amid the drama at The Angle.
fixes.repl:
Stuart's cavalry fought Gregg's Union cavalry division and Custer's Michigan brigade east of the town. Pleasonton's report says a heavy force of cavalry attempted to gain the Union rear and was defeated by Gregg, with several fine charges by the 1st Michigan Cavalry (OR 27/1 p.916). Lee's report says the cavalry effectually protected the Confederate left and that Hampton was seriously wounded.

Custer is reported to have led a Michigan regiment against Hampton's brigade at a gallop, shouting "Come on, you Wolverines!" — a report from veterans' later accounts.

Witnesses later reported that Lee rode among the survivors and took the blame on himself. It was the last great Confederate effort of the battle.

fixes.src: time-facts R005 (HistoryNet, Stone Sentinels, NPS marker); OR 27/1 p.1031 (Calef); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth, 5 a.m.)
fixes.find: "panel_summary": "At approximately 7:30am on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry fired the first shot of the Battle of Gettysburg. He borrowed a carbine from a sergeant, rested it on a fence rail, and fired at a distant Confederate officer. The shot missed -- but 51,000 casualties would follow."
fixes.repl: "panel_summary": "About 7:30 a.m. on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry is traditionally credited with the first shot of the battle, fired from a borrowed carbine at a Confederate officer on the Chambersburg Pike. Other men claimed earlier shots, so the claim is contested; the Official Records credit Lieutenant Roder's gun of Calef's battery with the first artillery shot."

fixes.before: first shot stated as fact; Corporal Hodges as the one who spotted the column (he is a rival claimant); "700 yards"; "51,000 casualties"
fixes.src: time-facts R005 (HistoryNet, Stone Sentinels, NPS marker); OR 27/1 p.1031 (Calef); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth, 5 a.m.)
fixes.find:
"full_script": "The morning of July 1 was warm and hazy when Corporal Alphonso Hodges spotted movement on the Chambersburg Pike. He reported to his sergeant: Confederate infantry, coming in force.

Lieutenant Marcellus Jones, commanding the vedette post of Company E, 8th Illinois Cavalry, borrowed Sergeant Levi Shafer's carbine. He rested the barrel on a fence rail along the Knoxlyn Ridge. In the distance, perhaps 700 yards away, a mounted Confederate officer rode along the pike ahead of his advancing column.

Jones squeezed the trigger.

The shot missed. The officer rode on. But the sound of that single shot rolled across the fields and into the histories of both nations.

It was approximately 7:30 in the morning. The Battle of Gettysburg had begun.

Jones had no way of knowing what his missed shot had set in motion. He could not know that 51,000 men would become casualties on this ground over the next three days. He could not know that the shot he had just fired -- borrowed, aimed from a fence rail, and wasted -- would be commemorated by a monument that still stands on Knoxlyn Ridge today.

He rode back to report what he had seen. Behind him, Heth's Confederate division continued its march toward Gettysburg."
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Buford's pickets west of Gettysburg watched Heth's division come down the Chambersburg Pike on the morning of July 1. By tradition, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones, commanding a vedette post of the 8th Illinois Cavalry, borrowed a carbine from a sergeant, rested it on a fence rail and fired at a Confederate officer riding ahead of the column, at about 7:30 in the morning. A monument on the pike marks the place the tradition names.

Not everyone agrees. Men of other regiments later claimed to have fired first, some of them hours earlier; the account that examined those claims found them mistaken, because Heth's column had barely left Cashtown at five o'clock. Artillery has its own claim: in his report Lieutenant Calef of Battery A, 2nd U.S. Artillery, writes that 'Lieutenant Roder now fired the first gun (which opened the sanguinary battle of Gettysburg)' on the head of a column of Confederate cavalry.

Behind the shot Heth's division, which he says was ordered to move at 5 a.m., marched on toward Gettysburg."

fixes.before: "Meade had offered him command of the entire army three days earlier"; "never married ... Kate Hewitt" and "finest corps commander" as fact; "personally leading"
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.114 (Meade), p.245 (Doubleday: "about 10.15 a. m."), p.696 (Howard 11.15), p.702, p.727 (11.30); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth); ledger WSD-14. The offer of army command was Lincoln's, not Meade's, and is dropped
fixes.find: "panel_summary": "Major General John Reynolds, the finest corps commander in the Army of the Potomac, was killed at approximately 10:15am while personally leading the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Shot through the head, he fell dead from his horse. He was 42 years old. His death left a void in Union command that was never truly filled."
fixes.repl: "panel_summary": "Major General John F. Reynolds, commanding the left wing of the Army of the Potomac, was killed on the morning of July 1 as the Iron Brigade went into McPherson's (Herbst) Woods. Doubleday gives the hour as about 10:15 a.m., Howard's reports give 11:15, and the source of the shot is unsettled."

fixes.before: "Meade had offered him command of the entire army three days earlier"; "never married ... Kate Hewitt" and "finest corps commander" as fact; "personally leading"
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.114 (Meade), p.245 (Doubleday: "about 10.15 a. m."), p.696 (Howard 11.15), p.702, p.727 (11.30); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth); ledger WSD-14. The offer of army command was Lincoln's, not Meade's, and is dropped
fixes.find:
"full_script": "John Fulton Reynolds was, by nearly universal agreement, the best corps commander in the Army of the Potomac. Meade had offered him command of the entire army three days earlier. Reynolds had refused -- he wanted the freedom to fight without political interference. He had ridden ahead of his corps to Gettysburg that morning to see the situation for himself.

What he saw at the Seminary convinced him that the Union army had to fight here. He sent a courier galloping south: bring the I Corps forward at the double-quick. And then, because Reynolds was that kind of general, he did not wait at the Seminary. He rode forward to lead the attack himself.

The Iron Brigade -- his beloved Iron Brigade -- was double-quicking across the fields toward the dark woods of Herbst. Reynolds rode to their head. He waved them forward into the trees, shouting encouragement.

The shot came without warning.

It struck Reynolds behind the right ear. He fell from his saddle without a word. By the time his aides reached him, he was already dead.

He was 42 years old. He had never married. He had been engaged to a woman named Kate Hewitt; her name was found on a ring he wore. She had been waiting for him.

The Iron Brigade went into Herbst Woods and broke Archer's Confederate brigade -- the attack Reynolds had set in motion with his life. But Reynolds was gone, and the Army of the Potomac would fight the next two days without the man who might have made all the difference."
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "John F. Reynolds commanded the I Corps and, under Meade's orders, the left wing of the army (the I, III and XI Corps). Meade's report records that Reynolds was directed to occupy Gettysburg and that, on reaching it, he found Buford's cavalry warmly engaged with the enemy. He sent orders for the XI Corps to advance as promptly as possible and put the Iron Brigade into the woods west of McPherson's Ridge.

He was shot near the eastern edge of the woods as the Iron Brigade went in. Doubleday, close by, learned 'with deep sorrow' that 'our brave and lamented commander, Major-General Reynolds, had just been shot, and was no more', and puts it at about 10:15 a.m.; Howard's reports of the same day say 11:15, and his later report 11:30, which is when Howard was told. The cause is unsettled: Heth believed one of the first shells from Pegram's guns struck him, and the usual account names a sharpshooter.

Doubleday took the I Corps and Howard the field when he arrived. The Official Records do not say what Reynolds intended beyond his orders; he was killed within the first hour of the infantry fight."

fixes.find: "panel_summary": "Within minutes of Reynolds's death, the Iron Brigade's charge through Herbst Woods captured Confederate General James Archer -- the first Confederate general officer taken prisoner since Lee assumed command of the army. Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin personally seized Archer as he tried to escape across Willoughby Run."
fixes.repl: "panel_summary": "The Iron Brigade's counterattack drove Archer's brigade back across the Willoughby Run and captured Brigadier General James J. Archer, brought in by Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin, who was killed later in the day. Doubleday reported nearly 1,000 prisoners from Archer's brigade; Heth said Archer was lost with some 60 or 70 of his men."

fixes.before: "first Confederate general ... since Lee assumed command"; invented movement details; dialogue as fact; "Tennessee and Alabama brigade"
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.245 (Doubleday), p.274 (2nd Wisconsin); OR 27/2 p.638 (Heth)
fixes.find:
"full_script": "The Iron Brigade swept through Herbst Woods like a tide. Archer's Tennessee and Alabama brigade had advanced confidently that morning -- they expected Pennsylvania militia, not the best infantry in the Army of the Potomac.

The black hats changed everything. A Confederate soldier who recognized them shouted a warning: 'That's no militia -- that's the Army of the Potomac!' But it was too late.

The Iron Brigade's left regiments -- the 2nd and 7th Wisconsin -- swept south of the Chambersburg Pike and curled around Archer's right flank. Archer's brigade, caught in the flank, broke. Men streamed back toward Willoughby Run, some plunging into the water to escape.

Brigadier General James J. Archer was trying to cross the run when Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin grabbed him by the collar.

Archer was a small, sick man -- he had been ill for weeks and had no business commanding a brigade in the field. He looked up at the private holding him and said simply that he would not be taken.

Maloney held on.

Archer was brought to Doubleday, who had just assumed command after Reynolds's death. The two men knew each other from before the war. Doubleday extended his hand and said cheerfully, 'Good morning, Archer! How are you? I am glad to see you!'

Archer refused to shake hands. 'Well, I am not glad to see YOU by a damn sight, Doubleday.'

He was the first Confederate general officer captured since Lee had taken command of the Army of Northern V...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Meredith's brigade formed, right to left, the 2nd Wisconsin, 7th Wisconsin, 19th Indiana and 24th Michigan. Doubleday writes that it 'deployed en echelon without a moment's hesitation, charged with the utmost steadiness and fury, hurled the enemy back into the run', led by the 2nd Wisconsin in line.

'To it also belongs the honor of capturing General Archer himself. He was brought in by Private Patrick Maloney, of Company G. It is to be lamented that this brave Irishman was subsequently killed in the action.' The 2nd Wisconsin's own report says Archer was taken by Maloney 'and brought to me, to whom he surrendered his sword'.

The prisoner count is disputed. Doubleday says nearly 1,000, all from Archer's brigade; Heth says Archer fell into the enemy's hands 'together with some 60 or 70 of his men'. A much-told exchange between Archer and Doubleday, who had known each other before the war, comes from later accounts, not from the reports. By Doubleday's order the Iron Brigade was then withdrawn to the east side of the run and re-formed on the high ground."

fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.246 (Doubleday), p.275-276 (Dawes: "7 officers and about 225 men"; Blair; Waller; 160)
fixes.find:
"full_script": "Rufus Dawes had been a schoolteacher before the war. On the morning of July 1, 1863, he was commanding the 6th Wisconsin -- the largest regiment in the Iron Brigade -- and watching Davis's Confederate brigade sweep north past his position toward the unfinished railroad cut.

Dawes received orders to charge. He turned to his men.

'Six Wisconsin, advance!' The regiment stepped off at the double-quick, moving north across the Chambersburg Pike. The 14th Brooklyn -- red-legged Zouaves -- joined on their left. The 95th New York came with them.

Davis's men had ducked into the railroad cut for cover. It seemed perfect -- a ready-made trench running east-west. What Davis had not understood was that the western portion of the cut was fifteen feet deep. His men were trapped in a ditch.

Dawes's regiment hit the cut at a run. The fighting was vicious -- men stabbed each other with bayonets across a gap of feet, grappled over regimental flags, fired at point-blank range. But the Confederates could not climb the sheer walls under fire.

Dawes reached the middle of the cut and shouted across to the Confederate officer opposite him: 'Where is the colonel of this regiment?'

'Who are you?' the officer called back.

'I am Colonel Dawes of the 6th Wisconsin. I demand the immediate and unconditional surrender of this regiment!'

There was a pause. Then the Confederate flag dipped, and men began throwing down their arms.

Dawes captured 232 prisoners -- nearly...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Doubleday had held the 6th Wisconsin out of the Iron Brigade as a reserve. When Davis's Mississippians and North Carolinians drove back Cutler's right and threatened the rear of the brigade fighting in the woods, he sent it against their flank. Dawes brought it up at the double-quick, checked the enemy with a fire by file at about 40 rods, and found them taking refuge in the unfinished railroad cut. The 95th New York and the 14th Brooklyn joined on his left.

Dawes ordered the charge. 'When our line reached the edge of the cut, the rebels began throwing down their arms in token of surrender.' Major John A. Blair surrendered the 2nd Mississippi; Major Hauser reports sending to the rear 7 officers and about 225 men. The regiment's battle flag was taken by Corporal F. Asbury Waller. The 6th Wisconsin lost not less than 160 men killed or wounded.

Doubleday says two regiments of Davis's brigade were taken with their flags, the 147th New York was released and a gun of Hall's battery recovered, all in less than half an hour and before Howard arrived. Dawes's well-known exchange with a Confederate officer ('Where is the colonel of this regiment?') is from his memoir of 1890, not from his report."

fixes.find: "panel_summary": "Brigadier General Alfred Iverson sent his North Carolina brigade forward without skirmishers, without reconnaissance, and apparently without personally leading the charge. His men advanced in perfect alignment directly toward a stone wall behind which Baxter's Union brigade lay waiting. In minutes, approximately 500 of Iverson's 1,470 men were shot down in rows. The shallow graves of his men are visible as depressions in the ground at Oak Ridge to this day."

fixes.before: "approximately 500 of Iverson's 1,470 men"; "perfect alignment, no skirmishers"; flank volley; "never given another brigade"; graves "visible as depressions"
fixes.src: OR 27/2 p.553-554 (Rodes), p.444 (Ewell), p.342 page image (return)
fixes.find:
"full_script": "The field north of Gettysburg was quiet when Iverson's four North Carolina regiments stepped off. They moved in perfect alignment -- a textbook advance that would have drawn admiration on a parade ground. No skirmishers preceded them. No one had scouted the stone wall ahead.

Behind that wall, Baxter's Union brigade lay flat in the grass, waiting. The 12th Massachusetts, 83rd New York, 97th New York, 88th Pennsylvania, 90th Pennsylvania -- all pressed close to the ground, rifles ready.

Iverson's men had covered perhaps half the distance when Baxter's soldiers rose up behind the wall and fired.

The volley came simultaneously along a front of several hundred yards. Iverson's regiments were struck in the flank -- the wall ran parallel to their line of advance. Men fell in rows exactly as they had been marching, in perfect military alignment, because there had been no time to break formation before the fire swept through them.

About 500 men fell in the first minutes. Not wounded -- fell, shot, lying in the grass in the same lines they had been marching in.

Iverson, watching from behind, reportedly believed his men had surrendered. He sent word to Rodes that his brigade had thrown up the white flag in dishonor. It was not true. His men were not surrendering. They were dying.

When Union soldiers advanced after the battle to bury the dead, they found the bodies lying in such perfect order that little digging was needed. They buried them where they fe...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Rodes sent Iverson's brigade forward and gave O'Neal the order to attack at the same moment. O'Neal's brigade went in with only three of its regiments, in confusion and not in the direction Rodes had ordered, and was quickly repulsed; Rodes says O'Neal, instead of leading it, had stayed with the 5th Alabama, which Rodes himself had held back.

Iverson's brigade, Rodes reports, 'attacked handsomely, but suffered very heavily from the enemy's musketry fire from behind a stone wall along the crest of the ridge'. With O'Neal repulsed, Iverson's left was exposed: 'His men fought and died like heroes. His dead lay in a distinctly marked line of battle. His left was overpowered, and many of his men, being surrounded, were captured.'

Ewell adds that Iverson wrongly sent word to Rodes that one of his regiments had raised the white flag and gone over to the enemy. The Confederate return of casualties prints 130 killed, 328 wounded, 308 captured or missing and 820 in all for the brigade; its regimental rows add to 455 killed and wounded and 308 missing or captured, 763, so the table disagrees with itself. Iverson's strength is not given in the reports read."

fixes.find:
"full_script": "The charge of Gordon's Georgia brigade had swept everything before it. When it was over, when the Union line on Barlow's Knoll had collapsed and the Confederates were pursuing the broken XI Corps south toward Gettysburg, John Gordon rode over the ground his men had taken.

He found a Union general lying among the dead, shot through the body and left behind in the rout. The man was barely conscious.

Gordon dismounted. He raised the officer's head, gave him water from his own canteen, tried to make him comfortable. He asked if there was anything he could do.

The dying man -- it was General Francis Barlow, commanding the First Division of the XI Corps -- said he did not expect to live. He asked Gordon, if it were possible, to find his wife and tell her where he had fallen.

Gordon promised. He had the general moved to a shaded spot and left a Confederate soldier to care for him. Then he rejoined the pursuit.

Barlow did not die. Against all expectation, he recovered -- slowly, painfully -- and returned to command. He served through the rest of the war. He became one of the best Union division commanders at the Overland Campaign.

After the war, Gordon heard a rumor that Barlow had died. Barlow heard a rumor that Gordon had died. They never sought each other out.

Years later, at a dinner party in Washington, two men were introduced and recognized each other simultaneously.

It was Gordon. It was Barlow.

They had both assumed the other was dea...
fixes.repl: "full_script": "Ewell reports that Early ordered Gordon's brigade in on the left of Doles's, and that after an obstinate contest it 'broke Barlow's division, captured General Barlow, and drove the whole back on a second line'. Schurz writes that Barlow, who 'had been directing the movements of his troops with the most praiseworthy coolness and intrepidity', was severely wounded and carried off, and that the division passed to General Ames.\n\nGordon told another story many times after the war: that he found the wounded Barlow on the field, gave him water, promised to tell his wife where he lay, and that the two men met years later, each believing the other dead, and became friends. That account is Gordon's; some of its details have been questioned, and neither the reports nor the Official Records contain it."

"full_script": "Daniel Sickles was a politician, a killer, and -- in his own estimation -- a military genius. He had shot his wife's lover on the steps of the White House and been acquitted by reason of temporary insanity -- the first successful use of that defense in American legal history. He had wangled a general's commission despite no military training whatsoever. He had survived every disaster through audacity, charm, and a complete inability to recognize that he might be wrong.

On the morning of July 2, 1863, he stared at the ground his corps had been assigned and decided it was unsuitable. The Peach Orchard, a quarter-mile to the west along the Emmitsburg Road, sat on slightly higher ground. In Sickles's judgment, the Peach Orchard was the position he should hold.

He did not ask Meade. He did not request permission. He did not inform his commander.

Around 3:00 in the afternoon, Sickles moved his entire corps -- 10,000 men and dozens of artillery pieces -- forward to the Emmitsburg Road.

Meade discovered the movement and rode south in fury. He found Sickles sitting on horseback in the new line and demanded an explanation. Sickles began to explain. Meade interrupted: the position was untenable. The line was too long. The flanks were exposed. The corps should go back.

At that moment, Longstreet's guns opened fire.

'I will withdraw if you order it,' Sickles said.

'I do order it,' Meade replied. 'But the enemy will not allow you to.'

He was right. W...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Meade's report says the II and III Corps were directed to occupy the continuation of Cemetery Ridge on the left of the XI Corps. About 3 p.m. he rode to the extreme left to await the V Corps and 'found that Major-General Sickles, commanding the Third Corps, not fully apprehending the instructions in regard to the position to be occupied, had advanced, or rather was in the act of advancing, his corps some half a mile or three-quarters of a mile in front of the line of the Second Corps'.

Meade writes that he was explaining to Sickles that he was too far in advance, and discussing the propriety of withdrawing, when the enemy opened with several batteries in his front and on his flank and brought up columns of infantry in a vigorous assault. The hour of the advance is itself disputed: accounts put it anywhere from noon to about 3:30 p.m.

The III Corps fought hard in its advanced line; Sickles was wounded early in the action and Birney took the corps, and it was forced back to the line originally designed. Sickles maintained for the rest of his life that the advance had been right. Words attributed to him and to Meade at this meeting come from later testimony, not from the reports."

"full_script": "The sharpshooters of Berdan's regiment were the best shots in the Union Army. Recruited for their marksmanship, equipped with Sharps repeating rifles, dressed in green uniforms that made them harder to see in the woods -- they were an elite within an army that still largely fought in shoulder-to-shoulder lines.

On the morning of July 2, Sickles was worried about his left. Buford's cavalry had departed. There was open ground stretching south and west, and nobody knew what was on the other side of Pitzer's Woods on Seminary Ridge.

Sickles ordered Berdan to find out.

The 1st US Sharpshooters moved into the woods in skirmish order -- open files, each man moving independently, using cover. No solid lines. No drumbeats. Just green-coated men filtering into the dark trees.

They found Wilcox's Alabama brigade.

The firefight was sharp and brief. The sharpshooters fell back with their information: there were Confederate infantry on Seminary Ridge, south of town, already in position. Longstreet's corps was there.

Berdan returned with his report. Sickles had what he needed.

Whether the reconnaissance actually showed what Sickles claimed it showed -- a Confederate flanking movement about to swing around his left -- is a matter historians still debate. What is certain is that Sickles used it as justification for advancing his entire corps to the Emmitsburg Road without orders. Whether Berdan's intelligence warranted that response, and whether the advanc...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Berdan commanded the First and Second Regiments of Sharpshooters. His report says that about 7:30 a.m. he sent forward a detachment of 100 men who held the crest beyond the Emmitsburg road all day, and that about 11 a.m. Birney ordered another detachment of 100 sharpshooters, with the Third Maine as support, to feel the enemy and discover his movements.

'I moved down the Emmitsburg road some distance beyond our extreme left and deployed the sharpshooters in a line running nearly east and west ... We soon came upon the enemy, and drove them sufficiently to discover three columns in motion in rear of the woods, changing direction, as it were, by the right flank.' The Union force attacked on the flank and threw the Confederates into confusion; they rallied and attacked in turn, and Berdan withdrew under cover of the woods, 'having accomplished the object of the reconnaissance', and reported about 2 o'clock to Birney.

Which Confederate brigade he met is not named in his report. How much weight the reconnaissance gave to Sickles's later decision to advance is disputed."

"full_script": "Gouverneur Warren stood on the summit of Little Round Top and understood in an instant what was about to happen.

The hill was empty. Below and to the south, through his field glasses, he could see the glint of sunlight on rifle barrels and bayonets -- Law's Confederate division moving through the trees at the base of Big Round Top, angling toward the rocky slope where Warren stood alone.

If the Confederates took Little Round Top, their artillery would command the entire Union line on Cemetery Ridge from the south. The army would have to retreat or be destroyed. Warren sent aides galloping in every direction: get troops, any troops, get them up this hill now.

The first aide found Colonel Strong Vincent commanding his brigade on the road below. Vincent did not wait for formal orders -- he did not have time for formal orders. 'I will take the responsibility of taking my brigade there,' he told the aide, and immediately led his four regiments up the rocky face of Little Round Top.

Vincent placed his regiments himself, walking the ground with quick precision: 16th Michigan on the right, 44th New York in the center, 83rd Pennsylvania center-left, 20th Maine on the extreme left. He was explicit about the left: 'This is the left of the Union line. You must hold this ground at all costs.'

He said this to Colonel Joshua Chamberlain of the 20th Maine.

Within minutes of the last regiment reaching its position, Confederate infantry appeared at the base of...

'Passing to the southern slope ... Colonel Vincent indicated to me the ground my regiment was to occupy, informing me that this was the extreme left of our general line, and that a desperate attack was expected in order to turn that position, concluding by telling me I was to "hold that ground at all hazards." This was the last word I heard from him.'

The brigade's line, from left to right, was the 20th Maine, 83rd Pennsylvania, 44th New York and 16th Michigan. fixes.find:
"full_script": "Joshua Chamberlain had been a professor of rhetoric at Bowdoin College before the war. He had taught himself tactics by reading military manuals at night. On the afternoon of July 2, 1863, he had already repulsed five Confederate assaults on the left flank of the entire Union Army.

His regiment was nearly out of ammunition.

The 15th Alabama, under Colonel William Oates, had been trying to turn the 20th Maine's refused left flank for nearly an hour. Each time, Chamberlain's men had stopped them. But the cartridge boxes were almost empty. The men were telling their officers they had nothing left to fire.

Oates was preparing another charge.

Chamberlain had two choices: retreat, or attack. Retreat was unacceptable -- his orders were to hold at all costs. Attack with empty rifles seemed suicidal. But Chamberlain understood something Oates did not: the Confederates below were as exhausted as the men above. The 15th Alabama had marched twenty-five miles that day before climbing and assaulting the hill. If he could shock them with an unexpected counter-charge, they might break before they understood what was happening.

'Fix bayonets,' Chamberlain ordered.

The command passed down the line. The 20th Maine -- fewer than 200 men still standing in the ranks -- fixed bayonets.

'Charge!'

The regiment swept downhill in a right-wheel motion, pivoting around the center and sweeping south and west. Chamberlain led from the front, a pistol in one hand and ...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Chamberlain's regiment stood on the extreme left of the Union line. He saw 'a considerable body of the enemy moving by the flank in rear of their line engaged' and stretched his regiment to the left, taking intervals and 'refusing' the left wing so that it stood nearly at right angles to the right, 'thus occupying about twice the extent of our ordinary front'. The flanking column 'burst upon my left'; the fight went on at close range, with the line withering and ammunition running low.

'It was imperative to strike before we were struck by this overwhelming force in a hand-to-hand fight, which we could not probably have withstood or survived. At that crisis, I ordered the bayonet. The word was enough. It ran like fire along the line, from man to man, and rose into a shout, with which they sprang forward upon the enemy, now not 30 yards away. The effect was surprising; many of the enemy's first line threw down their arms and surrendered.'

'Four hundred prisoners, including two field and several line officers, were sent to the rear', he wrote, mainly from the 15th and 47th Alabama with some of the 4th and 5th Texas, and 150 of the enemy were found killed and wounded in front. The hour is disputed: accounts range from about 5:10 to after 7 p.m. Chamberlain received the Medal of Honor in 1893."

"full_script": "Winfield Scott Hancock had been riding hard along Cemetery Ridge for twenty minutes, trying to hold together a line that was dissolving in front of him. The III Corps was gone -- shattered, streaming back from the Peach Orchard and the Wheatfield. The gap in the Union center was real and it was widening.

Across the fields, Cadmus Wilcox's Alabama brigade was advancing at the double-quick toward that gap. If they reached Cemetery Ridge, the Union line would be cut in two.

Hancock turned in his saddle. The only regiment near at hand was the 1st Minnesota -- 262 officers and men under Colonel William Colvill.

'My God, are these all the men we have here?' Hancock said.

Then he ordered them forward.

Colvill understood what the order meant. He turned to his regiment: 'Forward, double-quick!'

The 262 men of the 1st Minnesota -- a state with fewer than 200,000 people -- charged into Wilcox's entire brigade.

The fighting was savage and brief. The regiment drove into the Confederate line with bayonets and clubbed rifles, and for a few minutes the Confederate advance actually stopped. The Alabamians had not expected this. They had not expected anything to be there at all.

But 262 men cannot hold long against 1,700. The 1st Minnesota was shredded. Colvill went down, shot in three places. The regimental commander, the lieutenant colonel, the major -- all hit. Companies were reduced to handfuls. The regiment fell back toward Cemetery Ridge.

But th...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Fox tells it this way. While Hancock was 'patching' up a second line he saw a column of the enemy, Willcox's brigade, emerge from a clump of trees near an unprotected part of his line. The First Minnesota, alone and unsupported, was near by, and Hancock, wishing to gain time until reinforcements could be brought up, rode to Colonel Colvill and ordered him to take the enemy's colors. A desperate fight followed in which the enemy was forced back, leaving their colors with the First Minnesota.

Hancock's own report says the regiment 'charged the rebel regiment in handsome style, capturing its colors, and driving it back in disorder', and that in its attack and its later advance it 'lost three-fourths of the officers and men engaged'. The timing was not accidental. The Union artillery on the hill could not depress their guns enough to fire directly at men climbing the steep slope below them. The light was failing. The Confederate attack would have to be met with musketry alone.

Hays's men swept up the hill with a ferocity that overwhelmed the XI Corps units defending the lower slope. They reached the crest. They seized the Union guns. "full_script": "Lee's report: 'On Cemetery Hill, the attack by Early's leading brigades, those of Hays and Hoke, under Colonel Avery, was made with vigor. Two lines of the enemy's infantry were dislodged from the cover of some stone and board fences on the side of the ascent, and driven back into the works on the crest, into which our troops forced their way, and seized several pieces of artillery. A heavy force advanced against their right, which was without support, and they were compelled to retire, bringing with them about 100 prisoners and four stand of colors.' Rodes was not in position to co-operate, and Early retired for want of the expected support.

On the Union side Carroll's brigade of the II Corps came up and drove the attackers off the hill."

For two hours, 170 Confederate guns had been firing at Cemetery Ridge. The Union guns had fallen mostly silent. To Alexander, watching from Seminary Ridge through the smoke and dust, it looked like the cannonade might have worked. The ridge appeared quieter.

But Alexander was running out of ammunition. The Confederate army had no ammunition reserve close enough to replenish the batteries before the infantry assault. When the guns stopped firing, there would be nothing left for close support.

He wrote his first message to Pickett:

'General: If you are to advance at all, you must come at once or I cannot give you proper support, but the enemy's fire has not slackened materially and at least eighteen guns are still firing from the Cemetery itself.'

Pickett showed the message to Longstreet. Longstreet, who had spent two days arguing against this assault, could not speak. He bowed his head.

Alexander watched the ridge. The Union guns were still silent. He wrote a second message:

'For God's sake come quick. The eighteen guns have gone. Come quick or my ammunition won't let me support you properly.'

Pickett came to Longstreet. 'General, shall I advance?'

Longstreet turned away. He could not order it. He bowed his head agai...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Alexander, who directed the Confederate guns, wrote in 1907 that he sent this note to Pickett at 1:25: "General: If you are to advance at all, you must come at once or we will not be able to support you as we ought. But the enemy's fire has not slackened materially and there are still 18 guns firing from the cemetery."

He had hardly sent it when he saw the Union fire fall off and guns limbered up and withdrawn. At 1:40, he writes, he sent another: "For God's sake come quick. The 18 guns have gone. Come quick or my ammunition will not let me support you properly." Alexander says he later learned that the first note reached Pickett in Longstreet's presence; Pickett handed it to Longstreet, who stood silent and turned away, and Pickett said, 'I am going to move forward, sir.'

Longstreet's own report says he found that Alexander had advised Pickett that the time had come, gave Pickett the order to advance, and found the supply of ammunition so short that the batteries could not reopen. Then 170 guns fired at once.

The sound was heard in Pittsburgh. Some accounts place it as far as Philadelphia -- 140 miles to the east. The smoke rising from Seminary Ridge was visible for twenty miles. Alexander had positioned his guns with extraordinary care. The Washington Artillery of New Orleans -- the most famous artillery unit in the Confederate army -- was in the line. Pegram's battalion fired from the northern end. Cabell's and Henry's battalions fired from the south.

fixes.find:
"full_script": "Alonzo Cushing was twenty-two years old.

He had graduated from West Point in 1861 and commanded Battery A, 4th US Artillery -- six three-inch rifles positioned directly behind the stone wall at The Angle, at the exact focal point of the Confederate assault.

The cannonade had been brutal for his battery. Horses killed. Men down. Two of his six guns disabled. By the time Pickett's infantry appeared at the tree line, Cushing had four guns serviceable and was wounded himself -- a fragment through the shoulder.

As the Confederate line crossed the Emmitsburg Road and came on, Cushing took another hit. The wound was grave -- a shell fragment through the groin. His sergeant, Frederick Fuger, urged him to go to the rear.

Cushing refused. He had two guns left. He would serve them himself.

With Fuger's help, he moved his last two guns to the wall itself -- the stone wall at The Angle -- and loaded them with double canister. As Armistead's men climbed over the wall on his left, as the Union line bent and buckled around him, Cushing fired one last round of canister into the Confederate infantry at a range of perhaps twenty yards.

He was shot through the mouth.

Fuger assumed command of what remained of the battery. The Angle held.

Cushing's family petitioned for a Medal of Honor for the next century and a half. The Army reviewed the case repeatedly. Bureaucratic obstacles -- the statute of limitations, administrative requirements -- delayed the award...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "Hunt's report counts Cushing's battery among those that 'had lost heavily in men and horses', with Cushing among the three battery commanders killed in the day's fighting. Webb, commanding the brigade he supported, writes: 'Lieut. A. H. Cushing, Fourth U. S. Artillery, fell, mortally wounded, at the fence by the side of his guns. Cool, brave, competent, he fought for an hour and a half after he had reported to me that he was wounded in both thighs.'

Another officer reports that Cushing 'challenged the admiration of all who saw him': three limbers blown up and replaced with caisson limbers under fire, wheels shot off and replaced, until, 'severely wounded himself, his officers all killed or wounded, and with but cannoneers enough to man a section, he pushed his gun to the fence in front, and was killed while serving his last canister into the ranks' of the enemy.

The story that he was shot through the mouth, and details of his sergeant's part, come from later accounts. Cushing was awarded the Medal of Honor in 2014 after a long campaign by his family and supporters."

They came in clusters and straggles, the survivors of a mile-wide charge across open ground under artillery and musketry. Some walked steadily. Some stumbled. Some were helping others walk. All of them had the look of men who had been through something that no words could explain.

"full_script": "Farnsworth had been promoted to brigadier general on June 29, four days before the charge. The ABT map dates the action to the south cavalry field at about 5:15 to 6 p.m.

Survivors later said that Farnsworth objected and that Kilpatrick answered sharply; the exact words are disputed and are not repeated here. Farnsworth led the brigade forward and was killed.

The question of whether the order was justified has been argued ever since; the reports read here do not settle it."

Colonize Silas Colgrove had received instructions to clear Confederate infantry from their position at the base of Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana were to charge across an open meadow -- perhaps 200 yards of ground fully exposed to Confederate fire from the woods beyond.

Lieutenant Colonel Charles Mudge commanded the 2nd Massachusetts. He read the order and then read it again.

He sent an aide back to Colgrove. Was the order correct? Had there been a mistake?

The aide came back. The order was confirmed.

Mudge looked at the meadow. He looked at his regiment -- 316 men who had served through two years of war, who had marched from Maryland to Pennsylvania, who trusted him.

He turned to his officers.

'It is murder,' he said. 'But it is the order.'

He drew his saber and led the 2nd Massachusetts across the meadow at the double-quick.

The Confederate fire from the woods was immediate and accurate. Men fell as they ran. Mudge was hit almost at once -- shot through the throat, killed instantly, falling in the open ground he had called murder to cross.

The regiment reached the Confederate position, could not hold it, and withdrew. In the few minutes of the charge and its aftermath, 136 of 316 men were casualties -- 43 percent.

The 27th Indiana charged alongside them. It did not go better.

Between his line and the enemy lay 'the open meadow, about 100 yards in width', and the enemy were sheltered by breastworks and ledges of rock.

He chose the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana. 'At the command, "Forward, double-quick!" our breastworks were cleared, and both regiments, with deafening cheers, sprang forward. They had scarcely gained the open ground when they were met with one of the most terrible fires I have ever witnessed ... It became evident to me that scarcely a man could live to gain the position of the enemy.' "full_script": "General John Imboden had been ordered to prepare for the retreat. He was waiting near Lee's headquarters when the survivors of Pickett's Charge began coming back across the fields.

Lee rode out to meet them.

He rode slowly along the broken line of men, and Imboden watched from nearby. What he saw, he wrote later, he never forgot.

Lee rode among his men and said to them, over and over: 'All this has been my fault -- it is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.' Some of the men reached up and touched his boots as he passed. Some wept.

That night, Lee found Imboden waiting for him.

'General,' Imboden said, 'this has been a hard day on you.'

Then Lee fell silent again. He seemed to be speaking almost to himself.

fixes.find:
"full_script": "The battle was over.

From the first shot on Knoxlyn Ridge on the morning of July 1 to the last cavalry action east of town on the afternoon of July 3, the Battle of Gettysburg had consumed three days and approximately 51,000 men. Seven thousand were dead. The rest were wounded or missing. The fields and orchards and woodlots of Adams County, Pennsylvania -- farmland, ordinary farmland -- were covered with the wreckage of two armies.

On July 4, while the town of Gettysburg tried to count its dead, the news arrived from the west: Vicksburg had fallen. Grant had split the Confederacy. Two disasters in two days.

Lee began his retreat on July 4 in a driving rainstorm. Imboden's wagon train -- seventeen miles of it, filled with wounded men who screamed with every jolt of the road -- moved south and west toward Virginia. The army followed, battered, depleted, but intact. Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. The opportunity to destroy Lee's army, if it existed, was not taken.

The Confederacy would fight on for nearly two more years. There would be Cold Harbor and the Wilderness and Petersburg and the Shenandoah and Appomattox. But the moment when Confederate victory was possible -- the moment when a successful invasion of the North might have forced a negotiated peace -- had passed on the afternoon of July 3 at a stone wall in Pennsylvania.

The copse of trees still stands. The stone wall has been rebuilt where it was torn apart in the fighting. A bro...
fixes.repl:
"full_script": "The battle was over. The Official Records print the Union loss for the campaign as 23,049 killed, wounded and missing in the revised return (3,155 killed, 14,529 wounded, 5,365 captured or missing), and the Confederate loss as returned as 20,451 (2,592 killed, 12,709 wounded, 5,150 captured or missing), which the editors call approximate. Later estimates are higher, notably Livermore's of about 28,000 for the Confederates, and the National Park Service gives about 23,000 and 28,000. The sum of 51,000 sometimes quoted is that rounded estimate. These counts include the wounded and missing; the figures for the dead alone differ again by source.

On July 4 Vicksburg surrendered. Lee's report says the heavy loss and reduced ammunition made another attack inadvisable and it was determined to withdraw: the trains with the wounded who could bear removal were sent to Williamsport on July 4, part by Cashtown and Greencastle under Imboden and the rest by the Fairfield road, and the army kept its position until dark and then marched in a heavy rain. Meade did not pursue closely.

The park preserves hundreds of monuments and markers; the number quoted in earlier versions of this page, 1,328, is the park's total for all monuments, markers and tablets, not for the monuments mapped here. The Angle and the copse of trees are preserved, and the wall there has been rebuilt."

fixes.before: Pendleton exercised little tactical control. Corps chiefs -- especially Alexander -- made the real decisions.
fixes.src: no report read supports the removed phrase
fixes.find: Pendleton exercised little tactical control\. Corps chiefs -- especially Alexander -- made the real decisions\.
fixes.repl: Pendleton was the army's chief of artillery.

fixes.before: Alexander's two messages to Pickett are among the most famous command communications of the battle. The cannonade consumed most of the Confederate ammunition...
fixes.src: no report read supports the removed phrase
fixes.find: Alexander's two messages to Pickett are among the most famous command communications of the battle\. The cannonade consumed most of the Confederate ammunition reserve\.
fixes.repl: Alexander commanded the First Corps artillery in the July 3 cannonade.

fixes.before: Alexander directed the July 3 cannonade and wrote one of the finest Civil War memoirs. His two messages to Pickett are definitive primary sources.
fixes.src: no report read supports the removed phrase
fixes.find: Alexander directed the July 3 cannonade and wrote one of the finest Civil War memoirs\. His two messages to Pickett are definitive primary sources\.
fixes.repl: Alexander directed the First Corps artillery in the July 3 cannonade.

fixes.before: One of the most famous artillery units in the Confederate army. Positioned
fixes.src: no report read supports the removed phrase
fixes.find: One of the most famous artillery units in the Confederate army\. Positioned
fixes.repl: Positioned

fixes.before: Latimer was only 19 years old. He positioned his battalion on Benner's Hill to bombard Cemetery Hill and Culp's Hill. The Union artillery response was overwh...
fixes.find: Latimer was only 19 years old\. He positioned his battalion on Benner's Hill to bombard Cemetery Hill and Culp's Hill\. The Union artillery response was overwhelming\. Latimer was mortally wounded\.
fixes.repl: Latimer, aged 19, placed his battalion on Benner's Hill to fire on Cemetery Hill and Culp's Hill; Ewell reports that he withdrew all but one battery, and Latimer was mortally wounded.

fixes.before: One of the most aggressive and talented Confederate artillerists. Posted on Herr Ridge July 1 in support of Heth.
fixes.src: no report read supports the removed phrase
fixes.find: One of the most aggressive and talented Confederate artillerists\. Posted on Herr Ridge July 1 in support of Heth\.
fixes.repl: Pegram's battalion was posted on Herr Ridge on July 1 in support of Heth.

fixes.before: Stuart's cavalry was absent July 1-2, depriving Lee of intelligence. Stuart arrived July 2 afternoon. July 3 East Cavalry Field is the major cavalry action.
fixes.find: Stuart's cavalry was absent July 1-2, depriving Lee of intelligence\. Stuart arrived July 2 afternoon\. July 3 East Cavalry Field is the major cavalry action\.
fixes.repl: Stuart reached the army on the afternoon of July 2; the cavalry fought at East Cavalry Field on July 3.

fixes.before: Stuart's controversial absence left Lee blind during the approach march. Lee reportedly greeted him with 'General Stuart, where have you been?' Stuart arrive...
fixes.find: Stuart's controversial absence left Lee blind during the approach march\. Lee reportedly greeted him with 'General Stuart, where have you been\?' Stuart arrived late July 2\.
fixes.repl: Stuart reached the army on the afternoon of July 2 (Lee's report). Accounts of Lee's greeting come from later recollections.

fixes.before: Hunt managed ammunition supply before Pickett's Charge -- deliberately silenced Union guns over Hancock's objections to conserve rounds. His decision is cred...
fixes.find: Hunt managed ammunition supply before Pickett's Charge -- deliberately silenced Union guns over Hancock's objections to conserve rounds\. His decision is credited with allowing Union artillery to devastate Confederate infantry during the charge itself\.
fixes.repl: Hunt was the army's chief of artillery. During the Confederate cannonade, at about 2.30 p.m., finding the ammunition running low, he directed that the Union fire be gradually stopped (Hunt, OR 27/1 p.239). His report counts 67 batteries with 372 guns (p.242).

fixes.before: A 6-gun battery online occupies roughly 42 yards of front. Total Union guns approximately 370 including horse artillery.
fixes.find: A 6-gun battery online occupies roughly 42 yards of front\. Total Union guns approximately 370 including horse artillery\.
fixes.repl: A six-gun battery is drawn occupying about 42 yards of front (a drawing convention). Hunt's report counts 67 batteries with 372 guns (OR 27/1 p.242).

fixes.before: McGilvery's emergency construction of the Plum Run Line on July 2 evening -- assembling guns from multiple batteries to plug the gap left by Sickles' collaps...
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.235 (Hunt)
fixes.find: McGilvery's emergency construction of the Plum Run Line on July 2 evening -- assembling guns from multiple batteries to plug the gap left by Sickles' collapse -- is one of the finest improvised artillery actions of the war\.
fixes.repl: McGilvery assembled batteries from several commands on the Plum Run line on the evening of July 2 (Hunt, OR 27/1 p.235).

fixes.before: Wainwright kept a superb diary -- one of the best artillery primary sources for Gettysburg.
fixes.src: no report read supports the removed phrase
fixes.find: Wainwright kept a superb diary -- one of the best artillery primary sources for Gettysburg\.
fixes.repl: Wainwright kept a diary of the campaign.

fixes.before: Osborn organized the massed artillery on Cemetery Hill that played a critical defensive role.
fixes.src: no report read supports the removed phrase
fixes.find: Osborn organized the massed artillery on Cemetery Hill that played a critical defensive role\.
fixes.repl: Osborn commanded the XI Corps artillery brigade and the artillery on Cemetery Hill.

fixes.before: Cavalry units fought primarily dismounted (carbines) on July 1, mounted actions July 3. Horse artillery batteries included as they operated integral to caval...
fixes.src: OR 27/1 p.167 (roster)
fixes.find: Cavalry units fought primarily dismounted \(carbines\) on July 1, mounted actions July 3\. Horse artillery batteries included as they operated integral to cavalry divisions\. Richmond's brigade slots are largely small detachments from other regiments\.
fixes.repl: Cavalry units fought mainly dismounted on July 1 and in part mounted on July 3. The records of 'Richmond's brigade' are small detachments from other regiments and do not correspond to a brigade in the Official Records roster.

fixes.before: VI Corps nearly all zero casualties -- army reserve. XI Corps routed July 1 north of town. XII Corps held Culp's Hill throughout all three days.
fixes.find: VI Corps nearly all zero casualties -- army reserve\. XI Corps routed July 1 north of town\. XII Corps held Culp's Hill throughout all three days\.
fixes.repl: VI Corps: 242 casualties in the return, mostly army reserve. XI Corps fell back through the town on July 1. XII Corps held Culp's Hill.
